Question¶

    Can Pitcher Statcast Data Help us find trends in Tommy John Surgery occurrences. Can this data reveal patterns that can help MLB organizations predict injury potential for Major League pitchers. Additionally, are there other trends we can reveal in the data that may allow MLB General managers to make better decisions with pitcher contract selections.

Describe what the variables mean in the dataset (Chapter 1).¶

- full_name is the name of the pitcher. 
- tj_history is a binary intiger of if they have undergone Tommy John surgery or not. The code 1 indicates Tommy John surgery. 
- age is the intiger age of the pitcher 
- innings_pitched is the maximum number of innings a pitcher has thrown in a season. 
- fastball_avg_speed is the average fastball speed in MPH from the pitchers best season. 
- fastball_average_spin is the average fastball spin in RPM from the pitchers best season.
- breaking_avg_speed is the average breaking ball speed in MPH from the pitchers best season. Examples include Curveball, Slider, Slurve, and Screwballs.
- breaking_avg_spin is the average breaking ball spin in RPM from the pitchers best season. Examples include Curveball, Slider, Slurve, and Screwballs.
- offspeed_avg_speed is the average offspeed pitch speed in MPH from the pitchers best season. Examples include splitters changeups and knuckleballs. 
- offspees_avg_spin is the average offspeed pitch spin in RPM from the pitchers best season. Examples include splitters changeups and knuckleballs.

# Download Thinkstats2.
from os.path import basename, exists


def download(url):
    filename = basename(url)
    if not exists(filename):
        from urllib.request import urlretrieve

        local, _ = urlretrieve(url, filename)
        print("Downloaded " + local)


download("https://github.com/AllenDowney/ThinkStats2/raw/master/code/thinkstats2.py")
download("https://github.com/AllenDowney/ThinkStats2/raw/master/code/thinkplot.py")

# import thinkstats2 package
import thinkstats2

# import thinkplot.
import thinkplot

# Build Histogram 
tj_hist = thinkstats2.Hist(tj_data_summary.tj_history, label='Tommy John Surgery')
thinkplot.Hist(tj_hist)
thinkplot.Config(xlabel='Tommy John', ylabel='Count', xlim=[0,1], xsacle=1.0)

    For the histograms below I need to evaluate those with and without TJ surgery. In order to do that I need to create two subsets of data with and without Tommy John.

# Create histogram buing matplotlib and 30 binsto improve readability. 
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


x = tj_data_summary.age
# Use 27 bins one for every age.
bins = np.linspace(18, 45, 27)

plt.hist([x], bins, label=['Age'])
plt.legend(loc='upper right')
plt.xlabel("Age")
plt.ylabel("Count")
plt.show()

# variance

# standard deviation

# age by tj 

x = no_tj.age
y = had_tj.age
# Use 27 bins one for every age.
bins = np.linspace(18, 45, 27)

plt.hist([x,y], bins, label=['No Tommy John Surgery','Has had Tommy John Surgery'])
plt.legend(loc='upper right')
plt.xlabel("Age")
plt.ylabel("Count")
plt.show()


#Print Means 
print("No TJ Mean: ", x.mean())
print("Had TJ Mean: ",y.mean())

# Import the library to perform T-test. 
import scipy.stats as stats

# Perform the two sample t-test to test difference of means.

t_stat, p_value = stats.ttest_ind(x, y) 
print("T-statistic value: ", t_stat)  
print("P-Value: ", p_value)

No TJ Mean:  29.125127161749745
Had TJ Mean:  28.75
T-statistic value:  0.3262498555948182
P-Value:  0.7443040679683057

    When evaluating the distribution of the age variable we see that it is quite skewed to the right, this is what we would expect as players can only ever the league at 18 and play as long as they are effective. We do not see any outliers and there is no apparent difference of means in age of players who have and have not had Tommy John surgery.

    When evaluating innings pitched, we see a pretty abnormal distribution. This can be explained by the difference between starting and relieving pitchers who play different roles on a team. We see this phenomenon in the large statistics for standard deviation (56 innings) and variance. Again, here we do not see any outliers as both the minimum and maximum innings pitched are reasonable and fair sample size to judge a pitcher's performance. There is no statistical evidence to support that pitchers who have had Tommy John throw less innings than those who have not.

# Build Covariance function. 

def Cov(xs, ys, meanx=None, meany=None):
    xs = np.asarray(xs)
    ys = np.asarray(ys)

    if meanx is None:
        meanx = np.mean(xs)
    if meany is None:
        meany = np.mean(ys)

    cov = np.dot(xs-meanx, ys-meany) / len(xs)
    return cov
In [70]:
# Build Pearson Correlation 

def Corr(xs, ys):
    xs = np.asarray(xs)
    ys = np.asarray(ys)

    meanx, varx = thinkstats2.MeanVar(xs)
    meany, vary = thinkstats2.MeanVar(ys)

    corr = Cov(xs, ys, meanx, meany) / np.sqrt(varx * vary)
    return corr
In [71]:
# Build Spearman Correlation Function. 

def SpearmanCorr(xs, ys):
    xs = pd.Series(xs)
    ys = pd.Series(ys)
    return xs.corr(ys, method='spearman')

Let's perform a series of difference of mean permutation tests to test if there is a statistical difference in the pitch stats (spin and speed) between pitchers who have and have not had Tommy John surgery.

# build a class to test the difference of means via permutation. 
class DiffMeansPermute(thinkstats2.HypothesisTest):

    # Test statistic is absolut dif of means
    def TestStatistic(self, data):
        group1, group2 = data
        test_stat = abs(group1.mean() - group2.mean())
        return test_stat

    # Record sizes of groups n & m and combine them to one array
    def MakeModel(self):
        group1, group2 = self.data
        self.n, self.m = len(group1), len(group2)
        self.pool = np.hstack((group1, group2))
   
    # Simulate null hypothesis by shuffling pooled values into 2 groups.
    def RunModel(self):
        np.random.shuffle(self.pool)
        data = self.pool[:self.n], self.pool[self.n:]
        return data

class DiffMeansOneSided(DiffMeansPermute):

    def TestStatistic(self, data):
        group1, group2 = data
        test_stat = group1.mean() - group2.mean()
        return test_stat

    Now let's perform a one-sided test to test the hypothesis that those with Tommy John surgery throw with less offspeed spin than those who have not had Tommy John surgery.

Analysis¶

    Here we can see that when we test the difference of means through permutation, we get a two-sided p-value of about 0.15 which means that we see a difference as big as the observed effect about 15% of the time. This p value is greater than .05 so we cannot reject the null hypothesis. However, when we perform a one-sided test we see a p-value of 0.065, Which is not statistically significant given the threshold of 0.05. However, due to the nature of a one-sided test we can infer that it is far more likely for the mean of offspeed spin for those who have had Tommy John surgery to be greater than those who have not. This information would be helpful to a general manager as it would give them some level of confidence that a pitcher with high offspeed spin may be part of a group that is subject to Tommy John surgery.

# Import package 
import patsy
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

# Build function to test variables  and return their rsquared

# Imput is df
def GoMining(df):
    """Searches for variables that predict pregnancy length.

    df: DataFrame of pitcher stats

    returns: list of (rsquared, variable name) pairs
    """
    variables = []
    for name in df.columns:
        try:
            #Test for variability 
            if df[name].var() < 1e-7:
                continue
            # Add variable to equation predicting Tommy John (tj_history)
            formula = 'tj_history ~ ' + name
            model = smf.logit(formula, data=df)
            #if model.nobs < len(df)/2:
            #   continue

            results = model.fit()
        except (ValueError, TypeError, patsy.PatsyError) as e:
            continue
        #Add variables to list allong with their accociated psuedo r squared. 
        variables.append((results.prsquared, name))

    return variables

Analysis¶

   After comparing all the models above none of the variables in our dataset is a statistically significant predictor of a pitcher needing Tommy John surgery. However, some of the models do provide a greater pseudo r-squared value meaning that they predict more of the variance that we see in the tj_history variable. Naturally the model with all variables produces the highest r-squared. All models produce the same accuracy though, given this one should chose the simplest model which is the model using only offspeed average spin as a variable. offspeed average spin is also the variable closest to statistical significance. In practice an MLB general manager could use this model to predict it a pitcher would require Tommy John surgery; however, I would be skeptical of the effectiveness of the model.

Summary¶

    The purpose of our project was to set out with pitcher performance data and information on their history of Tommy John surgery and find if there was a way through analytics that we could predict if a player would require Tommy John surgery or not. Secondly, we wanted to know if this data could provide us with any other insights into pitcher performance. This project was done through the lens of an MLB general manager trying to maximize pitching performance and mitigate injury risk in contract selections. 

    In the end the outcome of our EDA was mixed results. We found some promising statistical phenomena.  We found some evidence that as a group, pitchers who required Tommy John surgery threw with more offspeed spin. However, we were only able to establish statistical significance to a 90 % confidence interval as opposed the standard 95%.  

    When performing logistic regression model to try to predict if a player would require Tommy John surgery, we did find a model that was over 98% accurate. However, none of the predictors we used were statistically significant and explained less than 3% of the variability we see in the data. This model is not effective for a general manager to use to mitigate injury risk.  

    Finally, we did see through correlation analysis that as a pitcher ages fastball velocity decreases linearly. This information, although it may seem obvious, could give a general manager confidence in not signing an older pitcher as their fastball velocity may be compromised.  Contrarily, when performing correlation analysis between age and breaking ball spin there was found to be no relationship.  A general manager equipped with this information may choose to sign an older player who relies heavily on their breaking pitches. Their age is unlikely to affect the spin and effectiveness of the pitches and because the player is older, they may be able to sign them at a bargain  

    I feel like having variables around arm slot angles, as well as metrics like height weight and arm length would have been helpful in this analysis. It is possible that these metrics in combination with the ones available could have led to more powerful insights.  

    One assumption that was made was that I chose to evaluate based on players best pitching performance season.  It may have been more effective to evaluate from the pitchers most recent season or career average as it is likely that results may have been skewed due to one good year.  

    Some of the largest challenges through this EDA were primarily in getting the data sets to join properly. Compiling Tommy John data with Statcast data proved to be no easy feat. Additionally, I would love to return to this project and analyze with a larger sample group and more seasons of data. I feel that having a larger sample of pitchers with Tommy John could help strengthen our findings and potentially even build a survival analysis to predict when a pitcher will need Tommy John surgery.
